## Part 1 · 00:00

[00:00] What is a gospel? Hi everybody. My name is Robyn Walsh. I'm a scholar of New Testament and early Christianity and part of Paths in Biblical Studies. And this must seem like an easy question, but it actually is a little complex. So, let's break it down. Now, the term from which we get the word in English gospel, euangelion, was a Greek term in antiquity that existed for hundreds of years before it was ever taken up by any what we would call early Christian writers. And it generally could be translated as good news.

[00:36] Now, I remember in college coming across this word when I took a course on Euripides, for example. So, again, hundreds of years before early Christianity is on the scene, the term existed as almost like a reporting term for reporting something. So, you would maybe have somebody come in to a kingdom to see the leaders and to report to give the good news on favorable result from a battle. Something along those lines. So, the term good news, you could think of it as like a a term meaning reporting, but giving some information to somebody about events that had transpired.

[01:12] Now, the word appears in early Christian literature, what we consider early Christian literature, thinking chronologically first with the Apostle Paul. Now, Paul in his letters refers to his message that he is delivering in his letters as the good news. And so, you will see that translated generally as gospel, or good news will actually be translated into English with a little footnote in a study Bible that lets you know this is the word for gospel. And this makes sense. Again, it's reporting. So, he is talking to these different groups to whom he is writing and reporting on the good news.

[01:43] Now, the term also appears, again thinking chronologically, in the writings that we now call the Gospels. And these are lives of Jesus. So, stories that are essentially telling what we would call his biography and the events of his life, as well as his death and resurrection. And so, if you were to open up something like the Gospel of Mark, which is generally considered our earliest extant Gospel, it begins with something like the beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ. Now, there again, the term is euangelion, Gospel.

[02:20] Now, some people will say that once you see that term euangelion used in something like the Gospel of Mark, that marks the moment, no pun intended, when Gospel transforms from a Greek term that has the resonant meaning that we just talked about to an actual genre category, a kind of literature.

[02:57] But I would say that that's not actually the case until probably much later, 2nd century, late 2nd century perhaps, when we are looking at someone like say Irenaeus, who begins talking about the fourfold Gospel, or you start to have other church fathers begin to talk about and cite from these texts that we now call Gospels. Once that begins to happen in the aggregate, you start to have Gospel function as almost this umbrella term or this shorthand for what is going on in these again biographies of Jesus and these accounts of this quote unquote biography of Jesus.

[03:15] So, that's how I think we can draw a distinction between, or to answer this question, what is a Gospel? It is a term that existed for quite some time before it was picked up by people like Paul, like the so-called Gospel writers, and then it comes to be associated with a particular writing of reporting on Jesus' life and activities. Another thing to consider is that there are many other terms that have come to be strongly associated with early Christianity that also existed in Greek long before it was taken up by the Jesus movement. Another term is ekklesia.

[03:52] That is where we get our word for church in English. But it existed as a term meaning assembly or association long before Paul starts to try to establish his own. And so, these are the kinds of terms that we want to really be careful about when we start thinking about the context of early Christianity and again the resonances of some of these these words and what they might have meant to someone in antiquity who would have seen them not as wholly novel or unique or strange.
